lessons.title: Bigger than that
lessons.subtitle: Comparatives with -tar and az
lessons.grammarPointEn: Comparative adjectives with the suffix -tar plus az (than): kalāntar az (bigger than); the compared thing follows az.

slides.title: Add -tar
slides.body: To compare, add -tar to the adjective: kalān → kalāntar (bigger), khōb → khōbtar (better in speech; bihtar is more common). The thing you compare against comes after az.

examples.dari: خانه او از خانه من کلان‌تر است
examples.translit: khāna-ye ō az khāna-ye man kalāntar ast
examples.en: His house is bigger than my house.

slides.title: The order
slides.body: First the two things, joined by az, then the -tar adjective, then ast. Literally: 'X, from Y, bigger is.'

examples.dari: کابل از شهر ما کلان‌تر است
examples.translit: kābul az shahr-e mā kalāntar ast
examples.en: Kabul is bigger than our city.

exercises.dari: این کتاب از آن کتاب ___ است
exercises.translit: īn ketāb az ān ketāb ___ ast
exercises.en: This book is newer than that book.

exercises.dari: خانه او ___ خانه من کلان‌تر است
exercises.translit: khāna-ye ō ___ khāna-ye man kalāntar ast
exercises.en: His house is bigger than my house.

distractorsEn: Tea is as warm as water.

exercises.en: Kabul is bigger than our city.
exercises.translit: kābul az shahr-e mā kalāntar ast

exercises.dari: برادر من از تو کلان‌تر است
exercises.translit: barādar-e man az tu kalāntar ast
exercises.en: My brother is bigger than you.

distractorsDari.dari: برادر من از تو خوردتر است
distractorsDari.translit: barādar-e man az tu khurdtar ast

distractorsDari.dari: برادر تو از من کلان‌تر است
distractorsDari.translit: barādar-e tu az man kalāntar ast

lessons.title: The best of all
lessons.subtitle: Superlatives with -tarīn
lessons.grammarPointEn: Superlative adjectives with -tarīn, placed BEFORE the noun: bihtarīn dōst (the best friend), kalāntarīn shahr (the biggest city).

slides.title: Add -tarīn, move it front
slides.body: The superlative adds -tarīn — and unlike the adjective, it goes BEFORE the noun. bihtarīn is the special word for 'best'.

distractorsEn: He is a better friend than me.

lessons.title: My book, her name
lessons.subtitle: Possessive endings and khud
lessons.grammarPointEn: Attached possessive endings -am, -at, -ash, -emā, -etān, -eshān (ketābam = my book) as a shorter alternative to ketāb-e man; khud for 'own'.

slides.title: Stick it on the end
slides.body: Instead of ketāb-e man you can say ketābam — 'my book' — by attaching a short ending. Both are correct; the ending is quicker.

slides.title: khud — one's own
slides.body: khud means 'own' and works for any person: kār-e khud, 'one's own work'.

exercises.prompt: Match the two ways to say it

blocks.title: Time & Routine
blocks.subtitle: Clocks, habits, and what comes next

lessons.title: What time is it?
lessons.subtitle: Telling the hour
lessons.grammarPointEn: Telling time on the hour with sā'at: sā'at chand ast? (what time is it?), sā'at dū ast (it is two o'clock).

slides.title: sā'at + number
slides.body: sā'at means 'hour' or 'o'clock'. Ask sā'at chand ast? and answer with sā'at plus a number.

lessons.title: Always, sometimes, never
lessons.subtitle: How often you do things
lessons.grammarPointEn: Frequency expressions hamēsha (always), har rōz (every day), gāhē (sometimes), hargez + negative (never), placed before the verb.

slides.title: Where they go
slides.body: Frequency words sit before the verb: hamēsha (always), har rōz (every day), gāhē (sometimes). hargez means 'never' and pairs with a negative verb.

lessons.title: Tomorrow I'll go
lessons.subtitle: Talking about the future
lessons.grammarPointEn: Dari expresses the near future with the present tense plus a time word: fardā mērawam (tomorrow I go / will go); there is no separate everyday future tense.

slides.title: Present + time word
slides.body: For everyday plans, Dari uses the present tense with a future time word like fardā (tomorrow). No new verb form needed.

examples.en: Tomorrow I will go to Kabul.

exercises.en: Tomorrow I will go to Kabul.
Tomorrow we will read a book.
Tomorrow you will go to school.

lessons.title: Go! Read!
lessons.subtitle: The imperative
lessons.grammarPointEn: The imperative: be- + present stem (bura! = go!, bukhān! = read!); negative na- (naraw! = don't go!).

slides.title: be- + stem
slides.body: To give a command to one person, put be- on the present stem: raw → bura (go!), khān → bukhān (read!). For 'don't', use na-: naraw (don't go).

slides.title: Saying don't
slides.body: Swap be- for na- to forbid: naraw (don't go), nakhur (don't eat).

lessons.title: Please sit down
lessons.subtitle: Polite requests with the plural
lessons.grammarPointEn: Polite requests use the plural imperative (be- + stem + -ēd) with lutfan: lutfan bukhānēd (please read); the plural is polite even to one person.

slides.title: Add -ēd, add lutfan
slides.body: To be polite, use the plural command (be- + stem + -ēd) and start with lutfan (please). It is polite even when speaking to one person.

lessons.title: I want to go
lessons.subtitle: mēkhāham + the want-form
lessons.grammarPointEn: mēkhāham (I want) plus a second verb in the subjunctive (be- form): mēkhāham burawam (I want to go); the second verb has no mē-.

slides.title: Want + a second verb
slides.body: 'I want to go' uses two verbs: mēkhāham (I want) + burawam (go). This second form — be- + stem + ending — is the 'want-form' (subjunctive). It never takes mē-.

exercises.en: I want to read a book.
We want to go to the bazaar.

lessons.title: I can read
lessons.subtitle: mētawānam + the want-form
lessons.grammarPointEn: mētawānam (I can) plus a second verb in the subjunctive: mētawānam bukhānam (I can read); same be- form as with 'want'.

slides.title: Can + a second verb
slides.body: 'Can' works just like 'want': mētawānam (I can) + the be- form. mētawānam bukhānam — 'I can read'.

lessons.title: I must go
lessons.subtitle: bāyad + the want-form
lessons.grammarPointEn: bāyad (must) with the subjunctive: bāyad burawam (I must go); bāyad does not change form for person.

slides.title: bāyad never changes
slides.body: bāyad means 'must'. Unlike other verbs it stays the same for everyone — only the second verb (the be- form) changes for person.

blocks.title: Experiences & Joining Ideas
blocks.subtitle: The past deepens; sentences join up

lessons.title: I used to go
lessons.subtitle: Past habits with mē- + past
lessons.grammarPointEn: Past habitual/continuous: mē- on the simple past (mēraftam = I used to go / I was going), for repeated or ongoing past actions.

slides.title: mē- on the past
slides.body: Put mē- on a past-tense verb to say you 'used to' do it, or 'were' doing it: raftam (I went) → mēraftam (I used to go).

examples.en: I used to go to school every day.
He always used to drink tea.

exercises.en: I used to go to school every day.
He always used to eat bread.
I sometimes used to go to the bazaar.
You used to work every day.

lessons.title: I have gone
lessons.subtitle: The present perfect
lessons.grammarPointEn: Present perfect: past participle (past stem + -a) plus a short ending (rafta-am = I have gone); 3rd person is rafta ast.

slides.title: Participle + ending
slides.body: For 'I have done' something, take the participle (rafta, khurda) and add a short ending. For 'he has', it is participle + ast.

lessons.title: Doing and making
lessons.subtitle: Compound verbs with kardan
lessons.grammarPointEn: Compound verbs = noun + kardan: kār kardan (to work), zendagī kardan (to live), fikr kardan (to think), kumak kardan (to help); only kardan conjugates.

slides.title: Noun + kardan
slides.body: Many Dari verbs are a noun plus kardan. Only kardan changes; the noun stays put. kār kardan (work), fikr kardan (think), kumak kardan (help).

lessons.title: I know that…
lessons.subtitle: Joining sentences with ke
lessons.grammarPointEn: The conjunction ke (that) joins a main verb of thinking/saying to a full clause: mēdānam ke ō āmad (I know that he came).

slides.title: ke links two ideas
slides.body: Use ke (that) after verbs like 'know', 'say', 'think' to attach a whole sentence: guftam ke mērawam — 'I said that I am going'.

examples.en: I said that I am going to the bazaar.

exercises.en: I said that I am going to the bazaar.
distractorsEn: He said that he is going to the bazaar.

exercises.en: I think that he is a teacher.
exercises.translit: fikr mēkunam ke ō mu'allem ast

exercises.en: He said that he ate bread.
He knows that I am here.

lessons.title: A2 review
lessons.subtitle: Everything from this level, mixed
lessons.grammarPointEn: Mixed review of A2: comparatives, superlatives, possessive endings, telling time, frequency, future, imperative, modals with the subjunctive, past habitual, present perfect, compound verbs, and ke-clauses.

slides.title: You've come far
slides.body: You can now compare things, give commands, say what you want and must do, talk about habits and experiences, and join ideas with ke. These exercises mix it all.

examples.en: I want to go to the best city.

exercises.dari: خانه او از خانه من ___ است
